title: Supporting Student Transitions at ACG School Jakarta: A Holistic Approach
content_html:
Transitions are pivotal moments in a student's academic and personal journey. ACG School Jakarta is committed to ensuring that each transition is smooth, supportive, and enriching.

Whether moving from primary to secondary education, adapting to a new school, preparing for university, or shifting into the workforce, these phases shape their growth and future success.

A Strong Start: Welcoming New Students

The journey at ACG School Jakarta begins with a well-structured orientation programme designed to ease new students into their learning environment. These strategies ensure they feel a sense of belonging from the moment they step onto the campus, reducing the anxiety associated with starting at a new school. The school provides:

  • Welcome packs with essential information about the school, academic expectations, and extracurricular opportunities.
  • Pre-entry events, including school tours, meet-and-greet sessions with teachers, and integration activities to help students feel comfortable before their first day.
  • A buddy system pairing new students with existing students to offer guidance and foster social connections.

"Starting at a new school was nerve-wracking, but my buddy made me feel at home from day one. The teachers were so welcoming too!" – A Year 7 student.

Transitioning Between School Phases

Each academic phase brings new challenges and expectations. ACG School Jakarta provides structured support at every stage to help students adjust to these changes seamlessly.

Primary to Secondary Transition
The shift from primary to secondary education is significant, as students encounter new subjects, teachers, and learning methodologies. To support this, ACG School Jakarta offers:

  • A structured transition programme, where Year 6 students participate in secondary school taster sessions and meet their future teachers.
  • Academic workshops, which introduce secondary-level expectations in core subjects such as Mathematics, Science, and English.
  • Mentorship programmes, where secondary students provide peer guidance and reassurance to younger students adjusting to the new environment.

"Seeing the Year 6 students grow in confidence during the transition period is always rewarding. We ensure they feel prepared and excited for the next step." – Ms Joanne Dickinson, Head of Languages and Inclusion.

Secondary to IBDP Transition
The International Baccalaureate Diploma Programme (IBDP) is a rigorous and comprehensive curriculum that requires students to develop strong time-management and critical-thinking skills. ACG School Jakarta prepares students through:

  • Subject selection guidance, ensuring students make informed choices aligned with their strengths and career aspirations.
  • Skill-building workshops, including research techniques, essay writing, and exam preparation to equip students with essential IBDP competencies.
  • University and career counselling, introducing students to pathways for higher education and helping them align their goals with subject choices.

"The transition to the IBDP was challenging, but the workshops and teacher guidance really helped me manage my workload effectively." – A Year 12 student.

Supporting University and Career Transitions

As students prepare for life beyond school, ACG School Jakarta offers extensive career and university guidance. This ensures that students are well-prepared for further studies or professional careers. The support includes:

  • University application assistance, including personal statement guidance, interview preparation, and access to global university fairs.
  • Internship and work experience opportunities, allowing students to gain insights into their chosen career paths.
  • Alumni network connections, providing students with mentorship and professional advice from graduates who have successfully navigated similar transitions.

"Helping students secure placements in top universities is one of the most fulfilling aspects of my role. Seeing them succeed beyond ACG is a joy." – Mr Christopher Wilson, Head of University Counsellor.

Social and Emotional Support During Transitions

Beyond academic support, ACG School Jakarta prioritises students’ emotional well-being through:

  • Counselling services, offering one-on-one support for students managing stress, anxiety, or uncertainty about their transitions.
  • Mindfulness and resilience programmes, equipping students with strategies to handle change and build emotional strength.
  • Parent engagement sessions, ensuring families are involved in the transition process and can support their children effectively.

"Having someone to talk to when I was struggling with change really made a difference. The counselling team was amazing!" – A Year 10 student.

An Ongoing Commitment to Student Growth

Transitions are continuous throughout a student’s educational journey, and ACG School Jakarta remains dedicated to providing comprehensive, student-centred support. Through a holistic approach combining academic preparation, emotional support, and career readiness, the school empowers students to move confidently into their next phase of life, equipped with the skills and mindset for success.

"We don’t just focus on academics; we nurture students to be resilient, adaptable, and ready for the world beyond school." – Mr Myles D’Airelle, ACG School Jakarta Principal.

ACG School Jakarta is more than just a school; it is a place where students grow, adapt, and thrive at every stage of their journey, ensuring they leave as well-rounded, future-ready global citizens.

title: Best Recreation Parks and Centres for Kids in Jakarta
content_html:
In search of recreation parks and destinations located right here in the capital to kick back on holidays or the weekend? Looking to step up your sports game, enjoy a break with the family, or give your children the chance to play freely with their friends in a safe, urban environment?

From classic arcades and indoor parks, ice-skating and go-karting, to trampolining and bouldering, Jakarta has no shortage of interactive entertainment venues for a fun day out.

Arcades | Bouldering | Trampolining | Indoor Parks | Go-Karting | Ice-Skating

Arcades

Timezone

Staying true to its “Time for Fun” slogan, Timezone remains committed to delivering cutting-edge entertainment. Today, with over 78 venues across 23 provinces, it continues to set the standard for modern, upmarket entertainment with floor-to-ceiling windows, an intuitive layout, advanced tiered powercards, the Tizo balance system, and a vibrant vibe.

Every Timezone visit is filled with exciting adventures that bridges generations. These immersive experiences range from Virtual Reality rides that transport players into new dimensions, to Social Bowling, Laser Tag, Bumper Cars and arcade favourites like Claw Time, Maximum Tune 6RR, Maimai DX and Pump It Up.

Introduced in 2024, Timezone Café provides a comfortable and stylish space where guests can dine and play in one destination. Now available in Timezone Summarecon Mall Bandung, Timezone Summarecon Mall Serpong, and Timezone Pacific Place, the café serves freshly delicious meals and beverages.

For special celebrations, Timezone Party Rooms offer exclusive venues for birthdays, anniversaries, gatherings, and team outings. Available at over 19 locations nationwide, these rooms come with dedicated hosts, 90-minute playtime and e-tickets for all invitees, with packages starting at IDR 200,000 per person for ten guests at minimum. 

Launched in 2022, the Timezone Fun App makes Timezone the only family entertainment centre in Indonesia with a seamless app experience. It allows guests to register, reload powercards, check balances, and access vouchers — anytime, anywhere. 

Also, Timezone Indonesia ensures that with great value-for-money offers, such as reload bonuses of up to 150%, bundle packages featuring exclusive Timezone merchandise, and collaborations with renowned lifestyle and F&B brands — each visit is rewarding.

IG @timezoneid | TikTok @timezone_id | timezonegames.com

Bouldering

Indoclimb

Starting as a small community, Indoclimb was born from a desire to bring the thrill of climbing to urban dwellers who may not have easy access to natural climbing areas. Jakarta’s bustling energy reflects the challenges and rewards of climbing, making it a welcoming space where people of all backgrounds can gather, socialise, and stay active.

With Indonesia's unpredictable tropical climate, Indoclimb’s indoor activities ensure a consistent, comfortable environment, especially as Jakarta’s malls are centralised hubs for urban life. These make climbing accessible and inclusive for beginners, families and seasoned climbers alike. Additionally, malls offer amenities like parking, food courts and proximity to public transportation, making it easier for participants to incorporate climbing into their routines.

As to why more Jakartans should take up indoor climbing, Indoclimb explains that climbing is a full-body workout that improves strength, flexibility, and endurance while being fun and engaging to provide stress relief from the fast-paced city life. Helping people to focus, unwind and conquer personal challenges, climbing teaches life skills like problem-solving, perseverance, and confidence, making it rewarding beyond just physical benefits.

In 2025, Indoclimb continues to innovate with regularly updated hold trends and dynamic climbing routes to challenge climbers of all skill levels, such as more competition-style programs inspired by international events and plans to expand. They foster an even stronger community through social climbing nights, adaptive workshops, expanded classes, and exclusive competitions like the Carnival Boulder Series from 4-13 February and 16 February 2025, plus a Valentine Celebration on 14 February.

IG @indo.climb | +62 819 2828 4328 (WA) | allez@indoclimb.com

Trampolining

Bounce Street Asia 

Since February 2016, Bounce Street Asia has committed to creating a fun, healthy environment. As Indonesia’s largest trampoline park, its three main goals are to provide a safe play space for children to enjoy in Jakarta's bustling city life, to promote health awareness by offering an active alternative to gadget dependency, and to strengthen the parent-child bond through shared physical activities. 

At the end of February, Bounce Street Asia opened its new state-of-the-art Virtual Reality arena, featuring Archery VR, Slingshot VR, and Soccer VR. As virtual shooting and football simulations, they are designed to deliver an interactive experience while enhancing motor and cognitive skills like agility, teamwork, focus, and hand-eye coordination.

Special event packages are also for fanbase community gatherings, Halloween parties, and Bollywood events. The venue also has a Bounce School, which follows an Australian gymnastics curriculum led by PB Persani-certified pro coaches. It aims to strengthen the body, enhance agility and flexibility, boost immunity, improve posture, and develop children's social skills through structured physical activities.

Bounce Street Asia is open Mondays through Sundays, from 10am to 8pm. Entrance fees are priced at IDR 150,000 on weekdays and IDR 175,000 on weekends and public holiday. Additional charges include IDR 20,000 for socks and IDR 20,000 for three-hour locker use.

IG @bouncestreetasia | +62 851 7301 9424 (WA) | bouncestreetasia.com

Indoor Parks

SuperPark Indonesia

SuperPark is a Finnish all-in-one indoor activity park built to international standards. With branches in nine countries, the first SuperPark in Indonesia opened at the Pondok Indah Mall Street Gallery, followed by Puri Indah Mall II on 16 December 2024, providing fun physical activities for all ages that reflect its philosophy “Move with Joy”.

Spread across 1,460 square metres, SuperPark, comprises 20 play areas of global-certified interactive rides equipped with digital technology. The Adventure Area hosts Adventure City, Fly Rail, Pedal Car, Donut Slide, and Wave Slide, while the Freestyle Hall offers Trampoline Platform, Ninja Track, and Super Jump. In the Game Arena, visitors can try Hot Stepper, Seat Soccer, Super Hoop, and Super Pinball; hone their skills with Super Ball, Super Bowling, and Super Bowl; or try physical challenges like racing with Super Bikes, Super Move, Super Run, and Street Games Court. A Jump & Fun area offers more energising activities.

SuperPark at Puri Indah Mall II also includes the Super Re-Charge Café, which serves fresh slushies, customisable Korean odeng (fishcake soup), and three flexible party rooms with removable partitions, ideal for different types of celebrations.

Tickets cost from IDR 150,000 to IDR 220,000, or IDR 200,000 to IDR 270,000 depending on the day of the week, playtime duration, and membership. Packages for birthdays, school visits, and company team building are available from IDR 4.5 million to IDR 5 million. Until 16 December 2025, SuperPark offers an early bird discount of up to 20% for ticket purchases through Traveloka. 

IG @superpark_indo | TikTok @superpark_indo | superpark.id

Go-Karting

Pegasus Karting

With a modern concept and high safety standards, Pegasus Karting presents itself as a competitive and fun automotive entertainment destination. With a specially designed and challenging racing track, as well as high quality and performance electric karts, beginners to experienced racers can experience the adrenaline-pumping excitement of racing.

Pegasus Karting arenas are available and open daily from 10am to 10pm at Pluit Village Mall in North Jakarta; Alam Sutera in Tangerang, Banten; Resinda Park Mall in Karawang, West Java and BEC in Bandung, West Java. Go-karts are categorised as Junior, Beginner, Pro and Master, with various racing systems and modes described as Team Race, Time Attack, and Fun Race. More competitive racers, meanwhile, can look forward to events, tournaments and competitions like the Championship Programme. 

For the novice racer or driving aficionado, Pegasus Karting’s arenas can be utilised to sharpen their driving skills and reflexes, provide challenging and exciting entertainment for family or friends, or act as a training ground for aspiring professional racers.

It also offers a spacious and comfortable arena, a wide array of food and beverages options, and a comfortable waiting area with entertainment facilities. Safety is also a top priority, with a strict security system, helmets, safety equipment, and experienced security guards always at the ready. 

Tickets can be purchased on the spot to book a racing session, while prices and packages start from IDR 67,000 to IDR 110,000 depending on the day of the week.

IG @pegasuskarting | +62 812 1377 6000

Speedy Karting

One of Jakarta’s premier go-kart entertainment centres, Speedy Karting offers an exhilarating racing experience for all ages. Designed to deliver both fun and competitive racing, it provides a well-maintained environment for karting enthusiasts, families, and corporate groups. 

The track is designed with challenging turns and straightaways to provide an exciting yet safe racing experience. A fleet of high-performance go-karts are available to choose from, well-maintained and suitable for beginners and experienced racers alike. All riders are provided with helmets and safety gear, and the track is regularly inspected to ensure optimal safety standards. 

Speedy Karting is easily accessible in Jakarta, with branches on the eighth floor of Lippo Mall Nusantara (formerly Plaza Semanggi), BSD Extreme Park, and the fourth floor of Kuningan City. These convenient locations make Speedy Karting a great destination for thrill-seekers and casual racers. Venues are open from 2pm to 9pm on weekdays and 10am to 9pm on weekends and national holidays.

Tickets vary from IDR 65,000 to 80,000 for five minutes of go-karting on weekdays or IDR 90,000 on weekends, with Mondays and Tuesdays offering a Happy Hour deal for IDR 65,000. Meanwhile, ten  minute sessions range from IDR 150,000 on weekdays to IDR 170,000 on weekends.

Packages include single rides, group bookings, and special promotions available for events. Not only does Speedy Karting cater to individual racers for birthday parties and corporate gatherings, but it also offers customisable event packages for businesses, schools, and private celebrations.

IG @speedykarting | +62 8778 7110 258

Ice-Skating

Skyrink Jakarta - Mall Taman Anggrek

One of Indonesia’s largest and most popular ice-skating arenas, Skyrink Jakarta has become a favourite destination for ice skating enthusiasts, offering a world-class skating experience for beginners and professionals. Established in August 1996, it is located in Mall Taman Anggrek, West Jakarta, with easy access to food, shopping, and entertainment.

With its 1,248 square-metre rink, Skyrink provides ample space for skaters to practise and enjoy the sport. The rink is well-maintained to ensure a smooth and safe skating experience for all visitors looking for a fun recreational activity or serious training.

Skyrink operates on a per-session basis, each lasting two hours. Tickets are priced at IDR 110,000 on weekdays and IDR 145,000 on weekends and public holidays. Skate rentals are also available and are included with the entry price. However, additional costs may be incurred for other possible mandatory equipment, like gloves and socks, unless customers bring their own.

For those eager to develop their skating skills, Skyrink Skating School offers professional training programmes for all ages and levels. Whether you’re a beginner learning the basics or an advanced skater aiming to refine your techniques, experienced instructors are available to guide you. The school offers lessons in Basic Ice Skating, Figure Skating, Ice Hockey, and Speed Skating – Short Track.

IG @skyrink_jakarta, @skyrinkjakarta.official | TikTok @skyrinkjakarta.official | +62 21 564 2888 | +62 81 2879 98080 (WA) | skyrinkjakarta.net/wp | skate74.wixsite.com/skyrinkjakarta

Oasis Centre Arena GC

Oasis Centre Arena is the only ice-skating rink in Indonesia of international Olympic size standards. Located at AEON Mall Jakarta Garden City, it operates under OCA Group, which develops ice-skating facilities in Indonesia to support the needs of skaters there and to introduce the sport to the public. 

With an affordable price, anyone can enjoy an ice-skating experience at Oasis Centre Arena with facilities such as Skating Aid, lockers to store personal belongings, an alert Rink Guard, and so on. The rink also has a membership programme that includes special discounts and free ice skating. 

Beyond the best ice-skating facilities for sports and recreation, the programs at Oasis Centre Arena range from basic technique training for beginners to professional skill training for athletes. This aims to not only accommodate casual ice-skating lovers, but also Indonesian ice-skaters fostered by the Indonesian Ice-Skating Federation.

Moreover, Oasis Centre Arena has been selected to be the venue for the Skate Asia 2025 competition in August, which will bring together over 1,000 skaters from around the world. The competition will be held from 2 - 11 August 2025. 

IG @oasiscentrearena | +62 813-8887-0141

title: H3XPO Promotes Strategic Synergy Between the Hospitality Industry and Corporations
content_html:
On Friday, 23 May 2025, H3 (Hotel Public Relations Association) Indonesia held H3XPO, the first exclusive B2B exhibition organised in collaboration with PERHUMAS (Indonesian Public Relations Association) at Autograph Tower, Thamrin Nine Complex, Jakarta.

With the theme of ‘Connecting Hospitality & Corporate Synergy,’ the event was attended by members of both organisations, including hospitality industry players and corporate communication professionals. From observing the impact on hotel occupancy rates on both ends, due to Indonesia's government budget efficiency policies that limit government agencies from holding events at hotels, H3EXPO seeks to address the issue.

“PERHUMAS appreciates H3 Indonesia’s strategic initiative in organising H3XPO as a tangible form of collaboration between public relations practitioners and the hotel industry," stated Glory Oyong, its Deputy Chairperson for Public Communication and Public Relations. She noted the unique challenges the hospitality industry faced from the post-pandemic situation and government policy adjustments, though she also recognised the opportunities presented.

"Through this forum, we are encouraging the creation of new business connections between hospitality industry players and decision-makers in the corporate sector,” Oyong added.

Yulia Maria, Chairperson of H3 Indonesia affirmed that the synergy between the hotel networks of H3 members and PERHUMAS members from various corporations can open up new mutually beneficial collaboration opportunities. Maria declared, “By hosting a curated event, H3EXPO provides direct access to decision-makers involved in business travel procurement, corporate event organisation, and future strategic partnership opportunities."

For more information, follow Himpunan Humas Hotel Indonesia on LinkedIn and @himpunanhumashotel on Instagram.

title: Keraton at The Plaza Unveils Southeast Asian Debut of The Unbound Collection by Hyatt
content_html:
Keraton at The Plaza, part of The Unbound Collection by Hyatt, announces its official unveiling as a luxury locale in Jakarta, marking the brand’s Southeast Asian debut where it reimagines the grandeur of Indonesia’s royal palaces through a modern lens. 

With 137 guestrooms and suites, expansive accommodation is offered starting at 64 square metres, framed by soaring 3.86 metre ceilings and floor-to-ceiling windows that bathe each room in natural light. Keraton at The Plaza collaborated with renowned design firm Hadiprana to infuse each space with contemporary Indonesian sensibilities, like batik kawung carvings. 

Two dining spaces, The Club and The Lounge, exude a warm yet refined ambiance, ideal for lunches, dinners, or afternoon teas. Situated adjacent to the lobby, The Lounge acts as the hotel's living room where guests can enjoy a selection of gourmet pastries, premium coffee, and artisanal teas. Meanwhile, The Club on level 7 offers private meeting and dining rooms, a chef’s table experience, The Bar and a wide dining area, while showcasing rotating collections of Indonesian art and local bespoke tea blends.

For guests seeking a more theatrical culinary experience, Keraton at The Plaza introduces its Teppan Dining Experience, available every Friday and Saturday evening and Sunday lunch. With private teppan tables available for groups of four or more, smaller parties are welcomed to share the teppan experience with others. 

At the hotel, The Daily Keraton Experience series culturally connects local and international guests with the essence of Javanese heritage. Rooted in tradition yet accessible to all, these include the Keraton Art Tour, traditional dance and gamelan performances, coffee heritage masterclasses, and the family-friendly Sunday Fun Walk.

Situated within the Plaza Indonesia complex, Keraton at The Plaza places guests at the centre of Jakarta’s cultural, culinary, and retail landscape. In addition to room-charge privileges when dining at any of the seven restaurants and lounges at the neighboring Grand Hyatt Jakarta, guests benefit from direct entry to Club Olympus: a holistic wellness sanctuary accessible via a private passageway from the hotel’s sixth floor, which features a state-of-the-art fitness centre, a salt chlorinated swimming pool, lush garden spaces, and a tennis court.

To celebrate the momentous unveiling, World of Hyatt members can take advantage of the upcoming Global Offer sale on 3 July, offering up to 25% off stays when booked directly through Hyatt’s official channels.

"Keraton at The Plaza is a tribute to the rich traditions of Indonesia’s royal heritage reinterpreted for today’s global traveler," said Parveen Kumar, General Manager of Keraton at The Plaza. "We are proud to unveil this exceptional property, which embodies a deep respect for cultural legacy, translated through thoughtful design, personalized service, and a strong sense of place."

As the first Southeast Asia property under The Unbound Collection by Hyatt, Keraton at The Plaza embodies the brand’s spirit of individuality and sense of place. With its design, hospitality, and cultural storytelling, the hotel offers a stay both luxurious and meaningful. 

Keraton at The Plaza invites guests to explore a narrative of timeless elegance, where every stay becomes a chapter in a greater story. Rooted in heritage, elevated by design, and shaped by authentic moments.

title: Is Jakarta ‘Fit for Fitness?’
content_html:
With more and more Jakarta residents adopting active lifestyles, the city’s urban landscape must adapt to its citizens’ needs. What’s driven this massive increase, and is Jakarta ready to accommodate this new culture?

Strength in Numbers

In April 2025, the fitness tracking and social networking application, Strava, introduced Bahasa Indonesia as an official language on their platform. The update followed a period of significant growth for the app in Indonesia, recording a tenfold increase in users in the last five years. Women specifically showed a twentyfold increase.

Global 2024 data from the app also showed that 78 per cent of runs in South Jakarta were listed as ‘matched runs’, making it the city with the most group or community runs in the entire world. 

Sports tech companies can teach us a lot. Garmin, one of the most popular wearable sports tracking accessories, sheds more light on Indonesia’s fitness trends through their 2024 report. They recorded a 56% increase in HIIT (high intensity interval training), a 42% increase in pilates and 25% increase in strength training from the previous year, marking a wave of higher frequency activity, or indeed new fitness enthusiasts altogether.

But we don’t need statistics to notice the trend, the evidence is all around us, especially in Jakarta, where it seems that everyone has joined a run club, padel club, spin class, pilates centre or, at bare minimum, a gym. The Jakarta International Marathon doubled its participants in just one year, from 15,000 to 30,000 runners (2024 to 2025). Clearly, Jakartans are fully embracing a more active, wellness-leaning lifestyle, but what exactly is fuelling this?

The Covid Effect

It seems trite to always go back to the pandemic, but it was a significant catalyst in shifting the mindset and behaviour of the population. The increased risk of Covid-related issues from poor overall health must have struck a serious chord, and despite being a generally well-known fact, the pandemic made this reality more real, visceral and immediate, prompting a lifestyle change.

In parallel, those wealthy enough to take advantage of the pandemic’s empty streets took to cycling and running, starting a whole new wave of aspirational desire. As many of us know, Indonesia is afflicted by a cult of personality, and suddenly fitness was cool, the new form of social currency trickling down from the rich and famous. Global trends bolstered this with the rise of sports-related fashion, from athleisure to the latest Hoka and ON shoes, or the coolest sports gear. 

But such aspirations, if not put into practice are just pipe dreams. In a 2024 report, OCBC Ventura noted “Indonesians are extremely price sensitive when it comes to paying for tertiary needs, e.g. fitness classes and gym memberships.” What helped to mobilise Indonesians into action was income growth, particularly of the middle class, enabling people to finally ‘buy into’ the lifestyle, from memberships to attire. The same report adds another interesting factor: vanity, finding correlations between gym memberships and cultural importance of physical appearance in different regions – just look at the gym trends in Canggu, Bali, and one will see clear evidence of this.

Jakarta may have its own specific reasons outside of these social drivers, and that has to do with the experience of the city itself. Until recently, Jakarta has never been a city that fosters ‘quality of life’ for its citizens: it’s been built on commerce, the urban buzz, being a political centre and melting pot. Residents complain about the same thing: traffic, work-life balance, that claustrophobic feeling of being constantly indoors, both for work and socially.
Sport has become the cure for this ‘urban malaise’. It’s opened up social opportunities (more on this in the following feature story), allowed people to disconnect and be present, and it’s become a way to actually interact with their city. Cycling down Sudirman on Sunday morning’s car-free day, rooftop HIIT sessions after work, running around Gelora Bung Karno Stadium – finally, a physical connection with one’s environment. These experiences make up part of the ‘je ne sais quoi’ of enjoying life in the city.

The Active City

What urban design features most effectively promote active lifestyles in cities?

Widely-regarded features include pedestrian-friendly infrastructure, comprised of wide, safe and well-connected sidewalks, as well as plazas and car-free spaces. Cycling infrastructure, which isn’t only about protected bike lanes, but also bicycle access integration with public transport. Of course, there’s the need for abundant parks and green spaces.

So how does Jakarta match up to these guidelines? As of 2025, Jakarta's green space coverage remains very low, at approximately 5.36 percent of the city's total area (BAPPEDA, 2025). Even then, these spaces are inequitably distributed across the city with South Jakarta enjoying more access with 2,3 percent, with the lowest district being East Jakarta  at 0,01 percent. For comparison, Singapore currently provides 40 percent of green space to its citizens.

Indonesia’s Spatial Planning Act actually has a law on Green Open Space (GOS), Law Number 26 of 2007, setting the ideal at 30 percent of a city’s total land area, with 20 percent public space and 10 percent private space. The good news is that Jakarta’s Provincial Government has actually targeted figure this for 2030, with 21 GOS spaces planned to be built in 2025 alone (Berita Jakarta). Adding to this, in May 2025 they also announced plans to add 3,8km of dedicated pedestrian and cycling paths in their ‘Complete Streets’ development programme – this adds to Jakarta’s 11km of protected cycling lanes, much of which was developed during the pandemic after a massive 340% increase in cyclists citywide (ITDP, 2021).

These will be highly consequential for Jakarta’s everyday citizens. Speaking from experience, my own neighbourhood in Jagakarsa benefited from additional parks made during Governor Basuki Tjahaja Purnama’s tenure, and I’ve witnessed children, families, groups of women enjoy these spaces to play, organise group yoga and aerobics. It made me think, ‘What were they doing before these spaces existed?’ It’s proof that urban design plays a significant role in shaping behaviour, opening opportunities for citizens to be active and healthy.

This is a sentiment shared by Jakarta’s running and cycling groups, who feel like options are limited when it comes to running or cycling destinations. The majority will congregate at Senayan’s GBK sports area, which is becoming crowded, or wait until Car-Free Day which now hosts up to 1,78 million people every Sunday along Sudirman. At the end of June, Car-Free Night was launched, testing out a Saturday evening free of vehicles starting at 10pm, also along the Sudirman-Thamrin stretch.

The car-free day concept is clearly popular and successful in getting citizens to be active and outdoors, but this brings us back to the issue of equitable distribution. More areas need similar initiatives to improve access for regional citizens and decrease travel time for those already participating.

The Caveat

The elephant in the room is invisible. Whilst Jakarta is gradually developing its outdoor spaces, this positive initiative is somewhat dampened by the city’s poor air quality. 

In the first half of 2025, Jakarta’s air quality index (AQI) averaged between 70–80, fluctuating between 50 and 120 (aqi.in). For reference, US-EPA 2016 standards state 0–50 is Good, 51–100 Moderate, 101–150 Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups. This remains similar even on Sundays, where millions are out on the street, limiting equitable access to sensitive groups.

The good news is that the solutions to improving active lifestyles in the city will have parallel benefits for air quality too. Additional green spaces, increased pedestrian and cycling paths, additional car-free hours and the massive developments in integrated public transportation systems will likely contribute to decreased air pollution in the long run. But the lesson is clear, these two crucial aspects should be developed in tandem to ensure a better quality of life in the city. 

What’s Next?

Jakarta is still at the beginning of its active lifestyle awakening, with fitness participation nationwide still at 1% of the population, meaning there is still huge room for growth.

Jakarta’s highly social nature will likely see more people joining sports groups and communities, fuelled by FOMO (fear of missing out), bolstered by the increasing number of sports-related businesses which improves access and reduces prices. The proliferation of budget-friendly gyms (e.g. Fit Hub, FTL, Anytime Fitness) is a great example of this, as is the number of padel courts being built across Jakarta, which doubled between 2024-2025 (27 to 55 courts respectively) and is estimated to reach 250 courts by 2026.

This will have interesting effects on the economy too, with Indonesia’s sports economy reaching $2.3 billion in 2024 (Ministry of Youth and Sports), and the running footwear market alone projected to generate US 77.8 million this year (statista.com).

But this is more than just about being fit and healthy, this rise is about citizens reclaiming the city, carving out spaces and experiences that make life in Jakarta enjoyable, redefining the city’s previous focus on work, commerce and malls. I believe the next evolution of this will be in wellness, with new spaces and venues that help Jakartans reclaim not only their physical health, but mental and spiritual wellbeing too. Watch this space.

Download our latest edition now: The Active City

title: 10 Best Spas in Jakarta: Top Massage & Wellness Centres
content_html:
Looking for the best spas in Jakarta to melt away stress and recharge your energy? From luxury wellness retreats in South Jakarta to affordable massage spots in Central Jakarta and beyond, the city offers a rich mix of treatments to suit every preference. Whether you’re after a Balinese massage, a quick reflexology session, or a premium spa experience in a hotel setting, Jakarta’s spa scene blends traditional Indonesian healing with modern techniques to deliver total relaxation.

Day Spa | Luxury Hotel Spa

Best Day Spas in Jakarta 

Gaya Spa Wellness

Gaya Spa Wellness offers a haven of tranquillity in the heart of the city. Inside, soft lighting, natural textures and calming music create a space designed for deep relaxation out of the spas in Jakarta.

Drawing on nature and ancestral traditions, the spa focuses on detoxing, anti-ageing and sleep improvement. Treatments incorporate aromatherapy, essential oils, natural ingredients and herbal drinks, turning every session into a healing journey for mind and body.

title: InterContinental Bandung Dago Pakar Offers Peak Range of MICE & Wedding Facilities

For more exclusive meetings, the Executive Boardroom is also available. title: Bathing in Indonesia In Early Prints and Photographs
content_html:
Bathing and cleanliness hold a significant place in Indonesian society, closely connected to the country’s tropical climate, religious beliefs, social customs, and overall well-being. Bathing is not merely a hygienic practice but is deeply rooted in spiritual, communal, and cultural traditions.

When Europeans arrived in Indonesia from the 16th century onward, they were struck by the frequency with which Indonesians bathed—sometimes two or three times a day, which contrasted sharply with European habits at the time. A wipe, instead of a wash, was often the prevailing European standard for cleanliness at the time. For early Western printmakers and photographers, bathing scenes became a captivating subject, offering a glimpse into the everyday rhythms of life in the old East Indies. In this article, Sake Santema from Indies Gallery showcases a few of his antiques depicting bathing in Indonesia.

A Bridge Between the Sacred and the Everyday

From ancient springs to modern city spas, the Indonesian approach to bathing is a holistic practice that weaves together physical health, spiritual purity, social respect, and cultural pride, connecting past and present in daily life and celebrations. In Java and Bali, rivers and springs are sacred spaces for purification. Not bathing before visits or ceremonies is often considered disrespectful. Three rituals of bathing that are still being practised are described below:

Melukat - The Balinese purification ritual is a spiritual cleansing ceremony intended to remove negative energy and restore balance to both body and mind.

Siraman - In Javanese culture, bathing plays a role in key life events, such as wedding preparations, where the siraman ceremony involves family members blessing the bride and groom with water for purification.

Wudhu - In Islam, the predominant faith in Indonesia, ritual ablutions such as wudhu are performed before prayers and after certain life events, highlighting the relationship between physical and spiritual cleanliness.

Natural Ingredients for Cleansing

In many Southeast Asian cultures, they used natural alternatives to soap long before Europeans adopted it. Traditional ingredients like lerak (soapberry), coconut oil, jasmine, and other fragrant plants have been used for centuries in traditional cleansing rituals. The Indonesian word for soap, "sabun," originates from the Arabic word sābūn, which traces back to the Latin word for soap, sāpō. It likely entered through Arabic or Portuguese traders, a linguistic journey across cultures.

Coconut oil boasts a 4,000-year history, originating in Southeast Asia and the Indian subcontinent, where the coconut palm was hailed as the "tree of life." Coconut oil—known as “minyak kelentik” in Indonesia—served multifaceted roles: treating skin ailments, protecting hair against sun and salt, and playing a part in religious ceremonies.

As European traders introduced it to the West during colonial times, it sparked a global craze. By the 20th century, coconut oil had become a commercial favourite, used in soaps and cosmetics, cherished for its stability and cleansing powers.

Image above: An early print of a coconut tree, labelled in Latin, Malayalam, Arabic, and Sanskrit. Published in the year 1678 in the Netherlands, in a comprehensive record of the plant’s many uses. (Sake Santema Collection)

The Evolution of Spa and Salon Culture

The presence of spas and salons in almost every street is a hallmark of Indonesian infrastructure, the longstanding appreciation for bathing has led to a thriving spa and salon industry that blends traditional and modern approaches.

Treatments such as the Javanese lulur body scrub roots in ancient Javanese royal courts, where it was part of pre-wedding rituals and spa treatments for nobility, symbolising purity and beauty. The blend that typically includes turmeric, rice powder, sandalwood, and fragrant flowers, aiming to soften skin and evoke a sense of calm, are now accessible to people from all walks of life, and a popular wellness treatment, blending tradition with modern spa luxury. Other popular treatments include flower baths, herbal compresses, and aromatherapy, all inspired by time-honoured rituals and believed to offer physical, emotional, and spiritual benefits.

Bathing remains a vital practice that connects the past with the present and shapes the rhythms of daily life and special celebrations.

The antiques in this article are available for purchase through Indies Gallery, while high-quality reprints can be found at Old East Indies.

Indies Gallery & Old East Indies
Jl. Gambuh No.17, Denpasar, Bali
www.indiesgallery.com

title: Art Jakarta Papers 2026: A New Fair Dedicated to the Power of Paper
content_html:
There’s a new and exciting event unfolding in Indonesia’s contemporary art scene. Art Jakarta Papers, an inaugural fair dedicated entirely to paper-based art, is coming to City Hall at Pondok Indah Mall 3 from 5–8 February 2026, bringing together 28 galleries from Indonesia and across Asia in a four-day long exhibitions, installations, and public programmes.

The fair was conceived in response to a long-standing gap in how paper is positioned within the art ecosystem. Locally, works on paper– ranging from drawings, prints, photography, and artists’ books to research-based and archival practices –have often been treated as secondary, even though they form the backbone of many artistic processes. Internationally, however, paper-based practices have gained momentum through art fairs, biennales, and institutional exhibitions that recognise the medium’s intellectual and material value, as well as its accessibility. Art Jakarta Papers emerges as a platform that expands the existing ecosystem and places paper-based works on equal conceptual and economic footing.

“We hope that this edition will strengthen, deepen, and expand the appreciation and knowledge of art lovers, collectors, and the general public in Indonesia and the region regarding the various forms and achievements of contemporary paper-based art,” says Artistic Director Enin Supriyanto.

Alongside gallery presentations, the fair will feature solo showcases by Indonesian artists and a programme of curated talks that examine the evolving role of paper in contemporary practice. Visitors can expect a wide spectrum of approaches, from traditional techniques to experimental and research-driven works.

The first edition is supported by Lead Partners BCA and Sucor Asset Management, each presenting a Special Presentation. myBCA introduces myBCA Space, featuring a large-scale paper installation by Rudy Atjeh. Built from hand-cut paper, the work takes the form of a tree that symbolises the human journey, with roots, trunk, and branches representing different stages of life. At its centre stands a cube that reflects the importance of life and financial planning. Visitors are invited to add origami elements to the piece, allowing the installation to grow throughout the fair. Atjeh, who has worked with intricate paper cut-outs for over a decade, continues his exploration of sculptural paper forms that engage with cultural memory and symbolism.

Sucor Asset Management presents Sucor AM Corner in collaboration with Naufal Abshar, using chess as a metaphor for investment strategy. Six papier-mâché sculptures represent the chess pieces, each depicted as a character with a specific role. The installation is paired with “Chess Play”, a live, interactive experience where visitors can play against Sucorians at three levels of difficulty, reflecting different investment risk profiles.

Further support comes from Main Partner EDISII, which will present a selection of limited-edition fine art prints by Indonesian artists, created through close collaboration between the artists and the production studio.

Art Jakarta Papers will also host the SPOT section, featuring curated solo presentations of large-scale installations. This year’s SPOT will include works by Iwan Effendi, presented by ara contemporary, and the photography collective Ruang MES 56, presented by kohesi Initiatives. 

To extend the conversation, six panel discussions will be held on 7–8 February 2026, covering topics such as conservation challenges in tropical climates, international market opportunities, restoration practices, and paper as a site for experimentation.

The fair opens by invitation on Thursday, 5 February, from 3–9pm.
Public access starts on Friday, 6 February, from 3–9 pm, and continues until Sunday, 8 February, from 11 am–9 pm.

Tickets will be available from 21 January 2026 at artjakarta.com

title: New Restaurants in Jakarta 2026: Latest Openings [Updated]
content_html:
Indonesia's capital city presents world-class food and beverage offerings. The scene is constantly growing and evolving, and sometimes it is hard to keep up. That's why we present a highlight of the best new restaurants in Jakarta 2026 to help you stay in the loop of the latest and most noteworthy openings. From fresh new cafés to late-night speakeasies and top fine dining venues, this list will help you to explore the superb dining scene across the city.

Browse new restaurants in Jakarta by month:

JANUARY | FEBRUARY | MARCH | APRIL | MAY | JUNE | JULY | AUGUST

We’ll be updating this article every month, so make sure to subscribe to our newsletter to stay in the loop with all the new restaurants in Jakarta! 

August Update

New restaurants in Jakarta that opened in August 2026

Kembang Goeyang

Kembang Goeyang brings a fresh take on Peranakan dining to Jakarta, offering familiar flavours in a relaxed, contemporary setting. Located on the ground floor of Sarinah, the all-day restaurant features a playful interpretation of Peranakan aesthetics, with a palette of white and blue accented by touches of pink, green and yellow. From patterned tableware to thoughtful tabletop details, the space balances heritage with a youthful sensibility.

The menu focuses on Indonesian Peranakan comfort food served in individual portions, making it equally suited to a quick meal or a leisurely dining experience. Dishes are arranged across charming sections including Tjemil-Tjemilan, Roti Rotian, Kuah-Kuahan, Nasi-Nasian, Ulek-Ulekan and Hidangan Penoetoep. Highlights include homestyle roti bakar in several flavours, alongside comforting savoury dishes and traditional accompaniments that celebrate the richness of Peranakan cooking.

The drinks selection follows the same balance of tradition and modern appeal, featuring signature coffee, teh tarik, matcha and es kopi susu gula aren. With its approachable format, nostalgic flavours and contemporary presentation, Kembang Goeyang offers a fresh way to enjoy Peranakan cuisine throughout the day – from breakfast and lunch to dinner.

Open daily, 10am–10pm; Sunday, 7am–10pm

Sarinah, Ground Floor, Jl. M.H. Thamrin No. 11, Central Jakarta | @kembanggoeyang

FOG Jakarta

Tagliatelle with miso and wagyu, tortellini served “like a ramen”, and ox tongue alla Milanese set the direction at FOG, a new Jakarta restaurant built around East and West cooking. The menu combines Italian foundations with Japanese and wider Asian ingredients.

The small plates options include a cannolo filled with steak tartare, bao with pork belly and kimchi mayonnaise, scallop tostada with wasabi emulsion, and Hokkaido oyster with green gazpacho granita. Starters continue with beef tataki and green peppercorns, ikayaki squid with edamame and black olives, and hamachi all’acqua pazza.

Pasta provides some of the clearest crossovers, here, diners can order tagliatelle with miso and wagyu, spaghettone with Asian greens and prawns, tortellini in dashi and roasted onion broth, or linguine with yuzu and lobster. Main courses include swordfish belly with XO emulsion, roasted black cod, charcoal king prawns and baby chicken with red miso and corn. Charcoal-grilled MB-7 and MB-9 beef is served with triple-cooked potatoes and bordelaise sauce.

For those who don't want to waste time scouring each of their extensive menus, FOG also has a weekday Vento Set, offering four courses with combinations such as egg and prawn salad, salmon consommé, mustard chicken thigh and miso dessert. Another option includes oxtail soup, gnocchi with pesto and cashews, crispy-skin salmon and fried milk.

Jl. Guru Mughni Kav. 10.3 No. 5, Kuningan, South Jakarta | +6281113021770 | @fog.jkt

Loong Dim Sum

Singapore-born Loong Dim Sum has opened its Jakarta branch in Menteng, serving halal dim sum, bao and Chinese favourites handmade by award-winning chefs. The contemporary restaurant caters to family meals, group dining and takeaway orders. Among its signatures is the Truffle Crystal Mushroom Dumpling, which combines mushroom and truffle in a thin, translucent wrapper before being steamed in bamboo baskets. The Special Dim Sum Set brings several house creations together in one order, with a mix of fillings, textures and cooking styles.

For sharing, the Truffle Roasted Duck is carved and served with crisp skin, tender meat and the aroma of black truffle. Other dishes include Mala Chicken with dried chillies and cashews, Sweet and Sour Chicken with pineapple, and Shrimp Paste Chicken Wings served crisp over shredded greens.

Jl. Purworejo No. 22, Menteng, Central Jakarta |  +62 811-1700-8866 | @loongdimsum_jakarta

Elio

Arka Group and Chef Aldo Volpi have opened a new Mediterranean restaurant in Senayan, serving coastal dishes, pasta and food cooked over an open flame. The grill leads the menu, with char-grilled octopus paired with chickpea purée, roasted paprika and herb gremolata. The Chicken Peri Peri is fire-roasted, served with peri peri aioli, and available as a half or whole bird for sharing. 

The seafood menu includes thinly sliced hamachi finished with Sicilian olive oil, burnt chive oil and charred olives, alongside Murray cod prepared over direct heat. Dishes arrive with deep charring, colourful vegetables, citrus and herbs adding contrast without overwhelming the main ingredients. For dessert, their Cast-iron Pancake is served warm with fresh berries and made for sharing, bringing the meal to a simple, generous close.

Ground Level, Sentral Senayan II, Central Jakarta |  +62 852-1801-2195 | @elio.jkt

July Update

New restaurants in Jakarta that opened in July 2026

Rin Culinary Art

Rin Culinary Art is a new dining destination built around a contemporary omakase format, pairing composed courses with a different tea at each stage of the meal. The menu draws on Japanese technique while allowing room for broader culinary references. One dish features local baby squid stuffed with prawn, basil and courgette, baked with Tuscan bread and arranged with a dark brush of sauce. Another presents Hokkaido scallops beneath a charcoal crust, paired with truffle and finished with crisp banana blossom.

Tea pairings distinguish the omakase further. Each course is matched with its own brew, allowing temperature, aroma and tannin to respond to the food as the menu progresses. Guests can expect the pairings to shift alongside grilled seafood, richer sauces and lighter finishes.

Jl. Wijaya II No 69, Melawai, South Jakarta | +628111586969 | @rin.culinaryart

JUN-KAI

JUN-KAI Japanese Eatery introduces a contemporary take on Japanese comfort food to South Jakarta. Open daily from 8am to 10pm, the new venue serves rice bowls, set meals and familiar flavours interpreted through modern fusion. Beef features prominently across the menu, their signature Beef Suki Don pairs tender slices of meat with rice and a glossy egg yolk, ready to be broken and mixed through the bowl. JUN-KAI Rice follows a similar format, combining beef, greens, kimchi and egg in a lidded clay pot that keeps the dish warm at the table.

For a fuller meal, the Steak Tataki Set arrives on a wooden tray with lightly seared beef, steamed rice, warm soup, fresh salad and several small side dishes. The arrangement captures the restaurant’s approach through generous portions, contrasting textures and a mix of savoury, fresh and lightly pickled elements. Its all-day schedule also makes it accessible for early meals, working lunches and later evening visits.

Jl. Pakubuwono VI No. 59, South Jakarta | +62 811 159 590  | @junkai.jkt

De Tiger

House of Tugu Old Town Jakarta poured the first drinks at De Tiger, a Far East speakeasy bar set within a colonial heritage building on Kali Besar Barat. The concept is inspired by the traders, mariners, and Peranakan communities that once shaped old Batavia, with Merem, a one-eyed Javanese tiger rescued by Raden Adjeng Kasinem in the early 1900s, as the bar's central character.

The cocktail menu unfolds across curated chapters referencing different facets of the era: 100 Karung Kopi is inspired by the coffee used to secure Merem's freedom, while Gedoeng Goelo Matjan pairs popcorn whiskey and marshmallow as a nod to Batavia's sugar trade. The food programme draws from Javanese, Peranakan, and coastal maritime influences, with dishes including the Midnight Katsu Burger with Curry Leaf Slaw. Evenings shift between live jazz and DJ sets.

House of Tugu Old Town Jakarta, Kali Besar Barat, Kota Tua | @detigerjakarta

June Update

New restaurants in Jakarta that opened in June 2026

Le Comptoir

Le Comptoir brings a French brasserie-style dining room to the Plaza Indonesia’s first floor. Born from the spirit of Le Quartier, the restaurant is designed for relaxed lunches, coffee breaks, dinners with friends and business meetings, with a space that moves from the Salon de Café into the main dining room, smaller seating corners and two private rooms.

The dining experience centres on three counters: Comptoir de Café & Patisserie for cakes, pastries, made-to-order desserts and hot drinks; Comptoir de Cuisine for seasonal dishes built around premium ingredients; and Cocktail & Speciality Comptoir for freshly prepared drinks. The menu covers brasserie staples, from Shrimp Croquettes, Fondue Parmesan with Duck Prosciutto and Saumon Façon Balik to Coral Snapper from the Arafura Sea, Joues de Bœuf Braisées, Contre Fillet Flambé and Tiramisu au Rum, Monté à la Minute.

Plaza Indonesia, Level 1, Jakarta | @lecomptoirjkt

Hakugin

Hakugin presents Japanese dining through teppanyaki, omakase and washoku to Fairmont Hotel’s 2nd floor. The restaurant provides private rooms, including a tatami room that accommodates up to 10 guests, suited for family meals, business dinners and small celebrations.

With a sushi bar as one of the highlights, guests can watch the chefs prepare seasonal sushi directly in front of them, as well as private teppanyaki rooms for live cooking. Dishes highlighted include Cold Somen & Abalone Carpaccio and fried amadai served with takenoko consommé soup, showcasing the restaurant’s focus on premium Japanese ingredients and precise preparation.

Fairmont Hotel Jakarta, 2nd Floor, Jl. Asia Afrika No.8, Senayan, Jakarta | @hakugin.jkt 

May Update

New restaurants in Jakarta that opened in May 2026

Yialos Taverna Menteng

Jakarta’s Greek-Mediterranean dining scene gains a larger and more family-ready address with the opening of Yialos Taverna Menteng. Located at Jl. Pasuruan No. 1 & 3, the new restaurant builds on the Yialos name with a broader menu, a dedicated seafood station, private rooms and facilities designed for longer gatherings. 

The restaurant is designed around the rhythm of a Greek taverna, with a spacious dining room, four VIP rooms for private occasions, a playground and a nursery room. It is a practical update for Jakarta diners who often look for restaurants that can handle different kinds of meals, ranging from business lunches and family dinners to celebrations with several generations at the table.

One of the main features is the seafood station, where guests can choose from fresh seafood and have it prepared to order. The menu introduces several dishes exclusive to the Menteng outlet, including Spicy Prawn Vongole, Kalamarakia Sti Skara, or grilled baby squid, Chickpeas with Sausage, Greek Fish Soup, Marides Tiganites, Crudo, Salt-Baked Fish, Grilled Fish and Kotopoulo Lemonato. The restaurant also continues to serve Yialos signatures, including Grilled Octopus, Meat Platter, Souvlaki and Athenian Lobster Pasta.

Yialos Taverna Menteng is open Sunday to Thursday from 8am to 10pm, and Friday to Saturday from 8am to 11pm.

Jl. Pasuruan No.1 & 3, RT.10/RW.5, Menteng, Central Jakarta Pusat | +62 811-8803-7088 | @yialos.id

Mallo Trattoria Italiana

Mallo Trattoria Italiana has opened at ASHTA District 8, bringing the team behind PICI to Jakarta with a new restaurant centred on fresh pasta, Italian comfort food and a polished casual setting. Located on the upper ground floor, the trattoria welcomes diners daily from 10am to 10pm.

The dining room combines deep red marble, dark timber and warm terracotta seating. Curved banquettes and cane-backed chairs create comfortable corners for lunch, dinner or a date, while the long open counter puts the kitchen’s daily pasta-making on display. Fresh pasta leads the menu with familiar choices including carbonara and slow-braised pappardelle ragù, joined by dishes such as cacio e pepe, fettuccine with truffle and squid-ink spaghetti topped with crab. 

Seafood also appears across the selection, from risotto and grilled fish to pasta served with shellfish. Recent chef specials have included a fish burger and eggplant parmigiana, giving regulars something new to consider between visits. Desserts continue the Italian theme, including tiramisu, while the restaurant’s wine offering makes it suited to a longer evening meal.

ASHTA District 8, UG-30, Jakarta | +62 822-6058-2860 | @mallo.jkt 

April Update

New restaurants in Jakarta that opened in April 2026

Dan's Diner

The essence of the American roadside eatery has taken root in Dharmawangsa. Born from a month-long journey through the authentic diners of New York and Los Angeles, Dan’s Diner stands as a fresh narrative from the creators of Dan’s Burgers.

The design leans into the nostalgia of a Hollywood film set. Chrome stools line the counter for solo visitors, while deep, high-backed booths encourage families to enjoy shared plates. The kitchen delivers a menu of pure American comfort food, intentionally avoiding local adjustments to preserve the original character of the dishes. This commitment to authenticity is most evident in the all-day breakfast selection, where airy buttermilk pancakes, crisp hash browns, and Nashville-style chicken and waffles are served from sunrise to sunset.

Its welcoming ambiance pulls in a mix of office workers in mid-day lulls and weekenders hunts for the perfect milkshake. This neighborhood staple offers an honest, down-to-earth vibe and a menu built for everyone, making it a go-to place for the Jakartans.

Whether you’re there for a quick bite or a long-overdue catch-up, this solid, hearty meal makes it easy to just sink into a booth and let the afternoon slide by. Dan’s Diners opens daily 7 days a week, from 11:00 AM to 10:00 PM.


Jl. Dharmawangsa Raya No.8a | @dansdiner.jkt

Sala Bistro Jakarta

The doors of Sala Bistro have swung open at Pondok Indah Mall 5, bringing a long-awaited breath of Balinese air to the heart of Jakarta. Named after the Spanish word for “living room,” the space is a masterclass in the art of the exhale.

Teaming up with the Honu Group, Sala landed in South Jakarta this past February. The space is light and airy, offering fifty seats that spread between a cosy indoor area and an outdoor terrace overlooking the park. With an open kitchen fueling a communal energy, the restaurant sheds any corporate stiffness.

The menu served early, beginning at 8:00 AM with an all-day dining experience that blends Asian and Western influences. The morning hours feature a curated brunch selection highlighted by the Sala McMuffin, a signature dish created specifically for the Jakarta location. For lunch and dinner, the offerings expand into the main dining service, introducing a diverse range of comfort food from Bone Marrow Fried Rice, Egg Chiffon to various pastas and their signature smoky, leopard-crust pizzas. This is also when the Salmon Tartare makes its appearance as the branch’s exclusive specialty. Coffee remains a central part of the identity, sourced exclusively from Bali’s Seniman Coffee Roastery.

Ground Floor, PIM 5 | @salabistro.jkt | +62 811 9989 3667

March Update

New restaurants in Jakarta that opened in March 2026

Little Frenchie Jakarta

After winning over Bali with its warm, unpretentious take on French dining, Little Frenchie has made its way to the capital. The neighbourhood French-inspired restaurant soft-opened at the end of February, with its grand opening on 6 March 2026, bringing the same community spirit to the city: refined in flavour, but relaxed in soul.

Born from a love for approachable cooking, Little Frenchie's philosophy has always been simple: food should move you. At the centre of the menu is Côte & Cru, a standout that presents T-bone steak in two expressions: one half transformed into a finely seasoned beef tartare, the other grilled to draw out the depth of dry-aged beef. Alongside it, French classics anchor the kitchen’s offerings: escargots in garlic parsley butter, a deeply caramelised French onion soup crowned with melted cheese, and duck confit, crisp-skinned and tender throughout. To drink, Little Frenchie proudly presents its French Spritz cocktails and a curated tap cocktail selection, a rare sight in Jakarta, adding a layer of innovation to an already considered experience.

As a neighbourhood restaurant, Little Frenchie Jakarta invites guests to return often: to gather, celebrate, and find comfort in cooking that feels both timeless and entirely its own.

Jl. Taman MPU Sendok No.9, Kebayoran Baru | @littlefrenchie.jkt

February Update

New restaurants in Jakarta that opened in February 2026

Baker Butcher Barista (B3) PIK

PIK (Pantai Indah Kapuk) has just welcomed its newest restaurant, Baker Butcher Barista, or affectionately known as B3. This new concept from MDA Restaurants (Carbón, Wabi-sabi, Animale) focuses on all-day dining, bringing together Jakarta’s favourite cuisines: artisanal baked goods, modern steak and grill, and speciality coffee. “From artisan baking with out-of-the-box flavours and a modern take on comfort food and steak, to speciality coffee handled with care, every element shows how we cook and create,” shares Andri Dionysius, Chef Patron of MDA Restaurants.

Making its home in the recently opened ADR Tower-Annex, the restaurant opens daily from 7.30 am until 9.30 pm – ready for any occasion. With pastries fresh from the oven every day, their Cempedak Flan (wild jackfruit egg custard) and Smoked Maling Pot Pie (house-smoked pork luncheon meat, mirepoix vegetable, green peas) are special favourites. For steak selections, indulge in Aged+Butchered’s ageing chamber, from Zabuton 9 to A5 Misuji, served with a choice of signature sides and sauces.

Furthermore, B3’s all-day dining menu offers comfortable classics with a unique twist, such as the fan-favourite Corny Bennie (an iteration of Eggs Benedict, with corn fritters in lieu of English muffins, with kaffir lime hollandaise) and B.Mw.–Cang (Bone marrow bakcang with wagyu shank and house-made chicken lapcheong). For coffee, their team recommends trying their Dji Sam Susu (a white Brew with clove, anise & cinnamon sugar notes) or the Black Calamansi (a Dark Brew with Fizzy Citrus Orange notes).

Open from 7.30am to 9.30pm daily.

ADR TOWER, ANNEX, Jl. Pantai Indah Kapuk I +6287722266784 I @b3.pik

January Update

New restaurants in Jakarta that opened in January 2026

Libros Jakarta

A new concept that celebrates tipples with literature arrives in Jakarta, high above the bustle. CasaLeña’s third floor glows with its own rhythm, inviting guests to a space designed for lingering conversations and crafted cocktails. At Libros, shelves of books line the walls, and the atmosphere borrows the vintage cocktail culture from Latin American lounges.

Within this backdrop, gatherings take on their own shape. The bar’s 60‑guest capacity allows for birthdays, brand launches, or private celebrations, with sofa corners and bar seating arranged to suit the mood. Flexibility is built into the design, ensuring each occasion feels tailored without losing Libros’ character.

As the rhythm continues through the week, Libros sets the soundtrack. Thursdays pulse with Tech House and Progressive, Fridays glide on R&B grooves, and Saturdays spark with karaoke and chart‑topping favourites. Each evening carries its own energy, balanced by a warm and intentional atmosphere. Guests can even shape the night themselves—bringing their own DJ or choosing from Libros’ selected playlists. The guiding ethos is clear: Your night. Your rules. Our bar.

Behind the bar, Ozy Ahmad tells stories in liquid form. His cocktail program respects the classics but adds inventive twists with signature creations such as Spicy Mathilda and Coco and the Coconut. Premium spirits and curated bites complete the experience, ensuring every glass feels considered.

With its literary‑inspired design and curated cocktails, Libros establishes itself as a destination for those who want their nights in Jakarta to unfold with stories worth retelling.

Casalena, 3rd Floor, Jl. Hang Lekir II No. 30, Jakarta I +62 813 184 8661 I @libros.jkt

Paris Café

From the group that brought us Paris Bistro comes a new dining venue that similarly celebrates French cuisine in Jakarta. Paris Café brings the nation’s quintessential café culture to the city, served in a setting inspired by the iconic Arts et Métiers metro station in Paris.

Perched along the popular eat street of Jalan Wolter Mongisidi, South Jakarta, Paris Café has been designed as an all-day dining destination, inviting patrons for coffees and pastries in the morning, to winding down over a glass of wine in the evening. café presents an iconic retro-steampunk aesthetic across the interiors, a design inspired by a very specific visual style from early 1900s.

When it comes to food, like at Paris Bistro, the menu offers a modern interpretation of French cuisine, as well as wider selections. The Brunch menu features classic French Omelette, Croque Madame and Monsieur, and a signature Lorraine Brunch Quiche. Whilst day and evening favourites may include the Chef’s Favourite Galette, Beef Cheek Ragù, Beurre Blanc Salmon  to Duck Confit. A menu of prime steaks is available for a heartier meal,  or comfort-favourite pastas, flatbreads and fresh starters make for go-to lunchtime staples.

As always with French cuisine, desserts are a must, of which there are many at Paris Café. The Milky Tapioca (artisanal milk ice cream, tapioca pearls and milk jam) and the Raspberry Pavlova are two standout favourites. This French connection is a very welcome addition to the slew of new restaurants in Jakarta.

Open from 9am to 11pm daily.

Jl. Wolter Mongisidi, +62 822 7777 8152 | @pariscafe.jkt

Aprez Locale

No stranger to opening new restaurants in Jakarta, the Amuz Group has expanded its dining portfolio with the opening of Aprez Locale, a relaxed, all-day dining concept now open on the ground floor of Citadines Sudirman Jakarta. Rooted in Asian flavours and designed for everyday comfort, the restaurant introduces a more casual expression of the group’s culinary philosophy.

Aprez Locale joins a well-established stable of Amuz Group brands, including Amuz Gourmet Restaurant, Artoz Bar, Aprez Catering, Aprez Café, and Caffe Tutti. This latest dining venue introduces a menu that centres on Asian-inspired comfort food, with many Indonesian favourites served. Highlights include Nasi Ikan Nusantara with Sayur Lodeh and Char Kway Teow, alongside a range of Western selections as well.

Designed with a relaxed yet contemporary atmosphere, Aprez Locale aims to become a neighbourhood favourite for hotel guests, professionals, residents, and city diners alike. Whether stopping by for breakfast, settling in for a business lunch, or winding down with friends over dinner, the restaurant offers an easy, welcoming space in the heart of Sudirman.

Aprez Locale is open daily for breakfast, lunch, dinner, and take-away at Citadines Sudirman Jakarta.

+6285285706736 | @aprezlocale.id | aprez.id

Vagabond

Perched on the 25th floor of Multivision Tower in Kuningan, Vagabond is a personality-driven cocktail bar shaped by global bar culture, creative expression and an instinctive read of the crowd. With intimate rooms orbiting a striking central counter, this bar’s design favours intention over trend. A space suitable for slow and relaxing evenings, accompanied by music that matches the distinct Jakarta energy. 

Co-founded by Michael Callahan, a widely respected name in modern mixology whose career spans Africa, Asia, Europe and North America, with long spells in island destinations from the Maldives to Bali. Working alongside Callahan is Payman Bahmani-Bailey, Vagabond Jakarta’s General Manager, whose résumé runs from New York and Los Angeles to Taipei and Singapore, with a stint in the Mediterranean. The pair previously collaborated at Proof & Company, helping define the culture behind the award-winning 28 HongKong Street.

At the heart of the bar is a tightly edited menu of 12 signature cocktails, supported by rotating modern and classic serves, visiting collaborations and three communal punch bowls that revive the convivial pleasure of shared drinking.

The drinks are expressive, occasionally provocative, such as Untitled (2025), a layered rum cocktail inspired by Jean-Michel Basquiat’s raw-meets-refined aesthetic; The Beagle, a freezer martini that evolves as a brined ice sphere melts, a quiet nod to Darwin and the poetry of change; and The Whizzer, clarified and carbonated, built with garam masala gin and chicken stock; surprising, savoury and oddly compelling.

A small stage anchors Vagabond’s evolving programme: DJs, curated music journeys and ritual-led moments that gently recalibrate the room. Vagabond joins Jakarta’s nightlife offering a worldly yet warm counterpoint within a city already rich with after-dark options. 

Multivision Tower, 25th Floor, Jl. Kuningan Mulia Lot 9B, South Jakarta I @vagabond.jkt

title: Mastering the Art of Sleep With Vishal Dasani
content_html:
Jakarta is a city that never slows down, and if you’ve ever tried to sleep through the roar of traffic, avoid the glow of screens, or resist the lure of late-night hangouts, you’ll know why rest feels elusive here. According to sleep coach Vishal Dasani, true rest goes beyond time spent in bed and calls for something deeper. 

“Normal sleep is just closing your eyes,” he says. “Restorative sleep is the kind that refreshes you, fills your energy, and makes you ready for tomorrow.”

A City That Never Sleeps

Groggy mornings—when coffee feels less like a ritual and more like survival—have become Jakarta’s silent epidemic. After energy is eroded by traffic, deadlines, and late-night scrolling, people wake foggy and drained. More time in bed, however, may not necessarily be the solution, with Vishal emphasising that the essence of rest lies in how restored you feel when the day begins, whether the night held seven or nine hours of sleep. 

“There’s no quality sleep without enough duration,” he points out, “but duration alone doesn’t guarantee restoration. The signs of quality sleep are simple: You sleep long enough, you don’t wake up too often, and you feel fresh when you open your eyes.”

Sleep itself follows a rhythm made up of distinct stages. Light sleep is when the body begins to relax and the brain quietly organises information from the day. Deep sleep is the phase of physical restoration, when tissues repair, energy stores are replenished, and immunity strengthens. Rapid Eye Movement (REM) sleep is the stage of vivid dreaming, where emotions are processed and creativity sparks. Together, these stages form the city’s full cycle of recovery, and missing one is like skipping a vital part of the day, Vishal explains.

Jakarta’s chaos often hijacks that rhythm, leaving bodies exhausted and minds restless. Vishal encounters many clients caught in what he calls hyperarousal. 

“People here struggle to slow down. They get into a state where the body is tired, but the mind is wired. They even overthink sleep itself; worrying about not sleeping becomes the very reason they can’t.”

Sleep Hygiene: The Real Upgrade

The path back to restorative rest lies in four everyday choices: timing, fatigue, relaxation, and environment. Vishal calls it the Three Plus One Formula.

 “Sleep comes when three conditions align: It’s the right time for your circadian rhythm, the body’s built-in clock that decides when you rest and rise; your body is genuinely tired; and you’re relaxed. The plus one is your environment—air quality, light, noise, temperature, even your pillow. Miss one of these and sleep quality drops.” 

He further elaborates that the real upgrade begins long before the lights go out. It’s sleep hygiene—the groove of daily habits—that sets you up for rest, so wake at a steady hour to train your body clock. Let morning light flood in, whether sunlight or a lamp on a grey day, and your brain knows it’s time to rise. Move your body as you would in everyday activities, and you’ll earn deeper sleep later. Eat with balance and you’ll build melatonin, the hormone that nudges you toward rest.

Coffee sharpens focus when taken early, but drink it too late in the day, and it lingers, stealing the night. By evening, the focus shifts to your room: cool, quiet, and softened by rituals, such as journaling, music, or a warm shower. Blend these habits, and they’ll turn sleep from struggle into renewal—the quiet upgrade that powers everything else.

Redefining Wellness Through Sleep

The encouraging sign is that awareness is growing. More Jakartans are beginning to see sleep as a necessity rather than a luxury. 

“Clients are increasingly aware of the importance of sleep,” Vishal shares. “They just haven’t found strategies that feel simple and sustainable. My role is to raise awareness and make the process easier.” 

As wellness culture expands in Jakarta, with fitness, nutrition, and mindfulness becoming part of everyday life, sleep benefits naturally.

The real recharge comes from sleep; the kind that resets your mood, sharpens your focus, and makes you feel unstoppable again. Vishal Dasani, who established WhiteNoise.id in 2021 after his own struggles with sleep sparked a deep interest in sleep science, reminds us that rest is the foundation of how we function every day.

Sleeping well means taking back control from the constant noise: waking refreshed instead of drained. And perhaps the boldest upgrade may not be a gadget or trend, but simply resting and letting the city wait until morning.

title: Living Galleries Land at 25hours Hotel Jakarta The Oddbird for Room Art Fair 2026
content_html:
This April, 25hours Hotel Jakarta The Oddbird flips the script on how art is shown. Turning its 10th floor into a corridor of galleries, the hotel debuts Room Art Fair 2026, timed with World Art Day.

For four days, from 16–19 April, hotel rooms shed their everyday function, becoming portals into different artistic worlds. Each door opens to a different gallery or artist, inviting visitors to wander freely and experience works at close range. Visitors may simply walk in and discover art at eye level.

The fair is staged with the Indonesian Art Galleries Association (AGSI) and brings together 13 galleries from across the country. The atmosphere is intentionally relaxed: artists, collectors, and guests mingle in spaces that feel more like conversations than exhibitions. With the support of Bank Rakyat Indonesia (BRI), the initiative also ties into the Ministry of Tourism’s vision of blending art, hospitality, and travel in ways that feel current.

The journey begins downstairs with Meet Me in the Lobby, curated by Zarani Risjad, where selected works greet guests in a casual setting. From there, the path leads upstairs, where each room — whether styled urban or garden — adds its own context to the art inside.

“This is about making art part of everyday life, closer to how people move through the city,” said Wibi Hananto, Assistant Director of Marketing Communications. The idea is echoed by AGSI, underscoring the fair’s commitment to accessibility and relevance in Jakarta’s evolving art scene. “It’s a step toward accessibility, showing art in formats that match how people interact today,” added Maya Sujatmiko of AGSI.

Rather than presenting a static display, the event highlights the dynamic interplay between creativity and environment. This approach aligns with the broader World Art Day programme at 25hours Hotel Jakarta The Oddbird, designed to spark dialogue and encourage exploration with fresh energy into the city’s creative ecosystem.

title: Nurturing Future-Ready Learners at BINUS SCHOOL Semarang
content_html:
Located on the northern coast of Java in Central Java, BINUS SCHOOL Semarang is designed to support both growth and global excellence. It offers a holistic approach to education, one that balances academic achievement with character development, while opening pathways that prepare students for an increasingly international future. 

In an era where education is often defined by grades and outcomes, BINUS SCHOOL Semarang presents a more considered perspective. As part of BINUS SCHOOL Education and a Cambridge international school, it places equal emphasis on academic rigour and the quieter, less visible dimensions of development: character, confidence, and a global outlook.

Set within a supportive and forward-thinking environment, the school presents itself not merely as a place of study, but as a community in which students are encouraged to grow into a fuller sense of themselves. Here, learning unfolds both within and beyond the classroom, shaped as much by daily interactions and experiences as by formal instruction.

For Rafisqy, now in Grade 10, this understanding developed gradually. What he once assumed would be just another stage in his education became something more nuanced over time. Through conversations that extended beyond lessons, challenges that demanded reflection, and moments that sparked curiosity, he began to see learning in a different light.

“For me, BINUS SCHOOL Semarang is a place that quietly shapes who I am, through small but impactful experiences in day-to-day school life,” he reflects.

A similar sentiment is shared by Rea, a Grade 8 student, whose journey has been defined by a growing sense of belonging. Arriving in a new environment can often feel uncertain, yet for her, it soon evolved into something familiar and reassuring, a place where she felt supported, both academically and personally.

“At BINUS SCHOOL Semarang, I found the confidence to express myself, explore my passions, and grow with the support of teachers and peers,” she says. “Beyond academics, it is the sense of community, encouragement, and shared experiences that make my journey meaningful.”

Taken together, these voices offer a glimpse into what distinguishes BINUS SCHOOL Semarang. It is not solely concerned with preparing students for examinations, but with equipping them for life beyond school: fostering resilience, independence, and a clear sense of identity.

In this way, education becomes less about a destination and more about a process. At BINUS SCHOOL Semarang, the focus is not only on where students go next, but on who they become along the way.
