title: Why Time Matters at Aged+Butchered
content_html:
At Aged+Butchered Jakarta, time is an essential ingredient.

Sure, a steak might be cooked and served in minutes, but what happens before it’s put to the grill is what really determines its flavour. At least, this is the philosophy that’s followed at Aged+Butchered, where quality meats are afforded much attention before they are ever brought to the table.

Serious steak lovers in Jakarta will be keenly familiar with this particular dining destination, which brings together two distinct cultures: the seriousness of an American steakhouse and the flair of an Asian yakiniku joint. In a city where loyalties are hard-earned, Aged+Butchered has stood the test of time since it opened in 2020, and speaking of time...

This is perhaps Chef Andri Dionysius’ most important ingredient. “A proper steak starts with an understanding of everything that happens before it is cooked,” explains the Chef Patron of MDA Restaurant, who has amassed one of the most impressive ‘meat libraries’ in the city at Aged+Butchered.

Whilst the restaurant places strong emphasis on sourcing some of the world’s most premium meats – Pure-bred Japanese Black Wagyu MS 9+ among them – it’s how the restaurant suitably ages and prepares them that makes all the difference. One could say it’s the steakhouse equivalent of ‘money doesn’t buy class.’

This is most visible in the ageing room, where selected cuts are left to gain depth, texture and character under carefully managed conditions. Some meats are dry-aged, enhancing the intensity of the meat’s characters, where natural nutty and umami flavours develop; whilst others are wet- aged, improving juiciness, tenderness and natural sweetness. These are aged anywhere between 30 to 180 days.

But the Chef and his team take things a little further, introducing their ‘Signature-Aged’ steaks, where more experimental processes develop unique flavours: like the 45-day Camembert-aged Ribeye, or others aged in whisky and port. The 365- day Wagyu Ribeye (Bone-in, MS7) is the longest aged selection in the restaurant, for those curious to know what Father Time can do.

The diverse menu has a meat for everyone’s fancy, with the ageing process coming to completion through tableside grilling, where diners can watch (and smell!) as their steaks sizzle, fat slowly and gorgeously rendering, to their preference of doneness. Pink Himalayan salt is the seasoning of choice, allowing each cut – and its age – to speak for its self.

Aged+Butchered remains a favourite amongst Jakarta’s steak connoisseurs, likely due to the restaurant’s dedication to its craft, promising a consistently high-quality meat experience. In 2024, the brand expanded to Canggu, Bali, where its continued philosophy has also built up a strong following among island diners. As restaurants come and go in Jakarta, this enduring steakhouse proves that, like its meats, things do indeed get better with age.

title: Merasa Origins: Tracing Java’s Ancient Wellness Traditions at Desa Potato Head
content_html:
Following the success of its inaugural chapter, India: Beginning with Balance with Reema Datta, Desa Potato Head is continuing its Merasa Origins series this September with its second chapter, Java: Entering Depth, taking place from 10-13 September 2026.

A three-part exploration of the cultural roots behind Bali’s wellness traditions, Merasa Origins traces a historical journey from India to Java and, ultimately, Bali. Across three four-day immersions, the series brings together practitioners and cultural voices to explore how philosophy, ritual and physical practice have travelled across generations and evolved through different places.

At the heart of the programme is merasa, the Indonesian word for “to feel”. At Desa Potato Head, this philosophy is reflected in an approach to well-being that is experienced rather than prescribed, bringing together movement, meditation, breathwork, traditional therapies, plant-based healing and sound practices.

The Java chapter turns its attention to the introspective traditions of ancient Jawadwipa. Guided by Tantric priest Pak Sugeng and spiritual anthropologist Serj Hunt, the four-day programme draws from Hindu-Buddhist Tantra and Javanese Kebatinan, exploring teachings and rituals passed down through sacred lineages.

Participants will move through morning practices, Javanese dance, collective mantras and workshops exploring Tattwa Tutur, the three forms of Broto and the principles of Right Relationship. Rituals including Yadnya, Upacara and a Tolak Balak ceremony offer deeper insight into Javanese approaches to devotion, protection and spiritual balance.

Rather than presenting these traditions as isolated techniques, Merasa Origins invites participants to experience them as interconnected systems shaped by history, place and community. The journey will conclude in Bali this November, completing the series and returning to the island where these layered traditions continue to shape contemporary approaches to well-being.
